As an example I have the common git commands, but just about anything will work. I'd like to hear ideas on how to make this more useful or comments that it's a horrible idea. When you send a command, to run/return/execute it you need to have the \n at the end. I know for most of you this is all common knowledge, but it wasn't to me.

 var terminal = require('child_process').spawn('bash');

 terminal.stdout.on('data', function (data) {
 console.log('stdout: ' + data);
 });

 terminal.on('exit', function (code) {
 console.log('child process exited with code ' + code);
 });

 setTimeout(function() {
 console.log('Sending stdin to terminal');
 terminal.stdin.write('git add --all && git commit -m "comment"\n');
 terminal.stdin.write('git push\n');
 console.log('Ending terminal session');
 terminal.stdin.end();
 }, 1000);
[node/io.js] Send commands to bash/terminal e.g. automated git

async.eachSeries( ['git add --all', 'git commit -m "comment"', 'git push'],exec,function(error,results) {
//More code if you want it after the terminal has done it's thing. Or just console.log that you got it done.
//results is an array of the stdouts of each command.
});

So you don't necessarily have to use async. You could just nest them a lot and that would give you more control on the handling of each function. Using exec does have the advantage of allowing you to stop when an error happens and nesting would allow you to customize that behaviour. For example do you really want to push if add and commit failed? Shouldn't it be git add && git commit && git push?

Also I would use exec to poll git status because trying to blindly push once every second is pretty crazy. Why not see what git status has to say first? You could also use a file watch. File watches return way to many events and you have to sort out what is what so it is a pain but you could do it.

I consider myself a Libertarian and I am registered. But I've found that I am just as much an Anti-Authoritarian, if not more, with a near visceral reaction to authority being forced upon me. What are your feelings on the subject?
Scale of 1 to 10; How Anti-Authoritarian are you?

After living in several states, both urban and rural areas, I find myself leaning libertarian. I'd say I'm an 8 on your anti-authoritarian scale. I am for absolute personal freedom and do not like the federal government. The problem is every anti-government person I meet is also completely detached from reality and believes Obama is a lizard antichrist Kenyan space alien who hates baby jesus.

Can't we be for states' rights and against the fed, and not be completely out of our damn minds?

EDIT: I'd like to include that my idea of "absolute personal freedom" is one that absolutely never infringes on the freedom of another individual. I didn't mean The Purge.

So your 8 is congruent to state's rights trump federal laws/government. I'm not disagreeing with you. Would you consider then a 9 would be cities right trumping states? 10 would be neighborhood rights trumping cities? I say cities as to mean populace subsects of states, and neighborhoods to mean subsects of those.

Yes I would say a city has the right to forego state law, an example being marijuana legalization/decriminalization. For me it gets fuzzier when it comes to smaller municipalities. In a worst case scenario, I feel a group of 20-30 individuals calling themselves an "independent neighborhood" would be able to institute some bizarre forms of abuse and torture if left completely to their own devices.

Here's an example of that: http://www.9news.com.au/world/2014/11/03/06/33/police-uncover-incest-sex-ring-in-alabama. I'm not sure I'm ready to live in a world where we don't take legal action against something like that because they've voted as a "neighborhood" that it's a good idea. Then again, I'm not sure how many people it takes for an electorate to make wise decisions.

You're running into a natural consequence of your political position. In order to be discontent with government interference you have to have a desired action the government is interfering with. This means that while the anti-authoritarian camp includes folks that have reasonable gripes with central authority, you also get everyone else that has an "abnormal" behavior that is not generally accepted by society. This means that you get the reptilian timecube crowd whether you like it or not. Sort of a baptists and bootleggers thing.

In terms of government? Almost 10. I think some voluntary authority can be useful, but all mandatory authority is bad almost all the time.

In personal life I'm fine with authority if it's genuinely warranted, like a teacher who genuinely knows more than me, but I can't stand it when it's unwarranted.
I am against overly-centralized power. Rather, I support checks and balances (beyond those which usually come to mind when this term is used). That is why I am not a libertarian.
